1.pericope_label: Put them in mind to be subject, and to speak evil of no man

schools.summary: Mark the turn before glossing a word: the charges so far had concerned Christian life among Christians, but there was a great life outside that little world, and the question is how the people of Christ were to regulate their dealings with it. Give the political history that made the reminder needful. The island had been some century and a quarter under Roman rule when Paul wrote, its previous government having been democratic; historians who have written of Crete dwell particularly on the turbulent and factious spirit of its people; and the many Jews who formed a large part of the Church there, always impatient of a foreign yoke, would in such an atmosphere be especially eager to assert their right to be free of Rome. Render the two nouns rulers and authorities rather than principalities and powers, since the latter word is used occasionally in the English version for an order of angels, and the terms here include all constituted governors and officials in the island. Note the grammar too, a remarkable double asyndeton with no conjunction between either the two substantives or the two verbs. On speaking evil, take the verb in its strong sense and then say carefully what it still permits, since we may be called to state what we know of a man's character: never for the purpose of injury or with pleasure taken in it, no improper colouring given and no circumstance exaggerated, never any attempt to charge bad motives on him since we know not what his motives were, and every palliating circumstance stated and given entire justice. And hear the whole charge as breathing the spirit of Christ, who when he was reviled reviled not again.

Guard the first noun against a misreading: it does not mean angels, good or bad, which are sometimes so called, but men in high places — the Roman emperor and senate, the consuls and proconsuls, and particularly those appointed over the island of Crete. Then give the reason the exhortation was needed. The Christians were not distinguished from the Jews by the Romans, and the Jews were reckoned a turbulent and seditious people, partly through principles privately entertained about not giving tribute to Caesar and partly through the insurrections of Judas of Galilee and Theudas; besides which there were many Jews in Crete, and the Cretians themselves were prone to mutiny and rebellion. Look past the island, too, to the constant difficulty: the apostles had great trouble keeping the common people subject, since we are all by nature desirous of power and no one willingly is subject to another; and nearly all the principalities of the world being then opposed to Christ, men thought them unworthy of receiving any honour. Extend the subjection demanded to edicts and laws and every part of civil government; and since magistrates were appointed for the preservation of mankind, hold that he who desires to have them removed, or shakes off their yoke, is an enemy of equity and justice and therefore devoid of all humanity. On speaking evil, forbid it not only of one another but of the men of the world, and of magistrates and persons in dignity, whose names are tender things and ought to be gently touched.

Identify the powers precisely: by the first word understand the Roman emperors or the supreme civil authority in any place, and by the second their deputies, the proconsuls and all such as are in authority under them wherever we dwell. Then explain why this doctrine was highly necessary for the Cretans, who were reputed exceedingly jealous of their civil privileges and ready to run into insurrection when they suspected any attempt to infringe them; and support it from an ancient fragment about Cretans who, fearing lest they should be punished, stirred up the populace by exhorting them to preserve carefully the liberty handed down from their ancestors. Then draw the distinction the fragment invites, which is the whole point of quoting it: to be jealous of our civil rights and privileges, and most strenuously to preserve them, is highly praiseworthy; but to raise a public tumult in order to avoid merited chastisement, under pretense that our civil privileges are in danger, is not the part of patriots but insurgents. Add that for such advice as is given here the known character of the Cretans is a sufficient reason. And on speaking evil, render it to blaspheme none, to reproach none, to speak nothing to any man's injury, but on the contrary to bear reproach and contumely with patience and meekness.

Begin with the office rather than the duty: ministers are the people's remembrancers, praying for them to God and preaching from God to them, since forgetfulness of duty is a common frailty and there is need of reminding and quickening. On subjection, hold that magistracy is God's ordinance for the good of all and must be submitted to not for wrath and by force only but willingly and for conscience' sake, whether the rulers be supreme or subordinate and whatever the form of government. Give the apologetic reason too: the Christian religion was misrepresented by its adversaries as prejudicial to the rights of princes and tending to faction and sedition, so that to put to silence the ignorance of foolish men, Christians must show themselves examples of due obedience — for the natural desire of liberty must be guided and bounded by reason and scripture, and spiritual privileges do not weaken but confirm our obligations to civil duties. On readiness to every good work, report that some refer it to what magistrates require and what promotes public tranquility, and grant this is included and perhaps first intended; but refuse to have it restrained there, since the precept regards doing good in all kinds and on every occasion that may offer, and mere harmlessness, or good words and good meanings only, are not enough without good works.

debates.question: What does readiness to every good work include?

sides.position: Whatever tends to good order and promotes public tranquility — included, and perhaps first intended, but not to be restrained there
It belongs with what precedes: all who do not refuse to lead a good and virtuous life will cheerfully yield obedience to magistrates
Prompt to perform all that is good, without restriction; a Christian should count it a privilege to have the opportunity

debates.question: Why did the Cretan church in particular need this charge?

sides.position: The island's turbulent and factious spirit under a century and a quarter of Roman rule, with a large Jewish population impatient of a foreign yoke
The Cretans were reputed jealous of their civil privileges and quick to insurrection, as an ancient fragment about them shows
The Romans did not distinguish Christians from Jews, and the Jews were reckoned seditious after Judas of Galilee and Theudas
Not Crete only: we are all by nature desirous of power, and the powers of the world being then opposed to Christ were thought unworthy of honour

outliers.note: Alone quotes an ancient fragment about Cretans stirring up the populace to preserve their ancestral liberty, and alone uses it to draw a distinction the passage invites: that jealousy for civil rights is praiseworthy, but raising a tumult to escape merited chastisement under pretense that those rights are in danger is not the part of patriots but insurgents.

Alone works out what the prohibition of speaking evil still permits when a man's character must be stated, setting conditions on colouring, exaggeration and the imputing of motives, and concluding that it is better we should have been mistaken about a man than that he should be a bad man.

Alone supplies a historical vindication of the charge, quoting the boast that when Julian summoned Christians to sacrifice they refused at all hazards but rushed to the front when he summoned them to fight for the empire, distinguishing their Eternal Lord from their earthly ruler.

themes: Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,
To speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men.

3.pericope_label: For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish: but the kindness of God appeared

schools.summary: Settle first whether the apostle includes himself, and do not assume it: there is no reason for confining this to Paul, since some things mentioned here were probably not true of him before his conversion and the connexion does not require it. He is stating why those Titus preached to should be urged to good lives, namely that those who are now Christians were formerly disorderly and sensual, so that the same gospel effectual in their case may be so in others. Turn the retrospect into a rule for preachers: they were not to be proud or arrogant but to remember they had been in the same condition as those they exhorted, and that what they had which was superior they owed to grace and not to native goodness — he will exhort the wicked to repentance most effectually who remembers that his own former life was wicked. Extend it beyond the pulpit, since when a Christian is tempted to unkind thoughts or words nothing is more appropriate than to reflect on his own past life. On the individual words, take deceived as something done to us, by the great enemy, by false teachers, by our own hearts and by the flattery of others, and note that it is characteristic of man to walk amidst constant though changing illusions — though the participle is passive, the middle is grammatically possible. And render the fourth verse exactly: the Greek word is philanthropy, the love of man, and the whole plan of salvation was founded on it.

Say what the retrospect is for: nothing has a greater tendency to promote humility and check pride in the saints than to reflect upon their past state and what they themselves once were. This is why magistrates, though evil men, are to be obeyed in things lawful, why no man is to be spoken evil of, and why every man is to be treated in a gentle manner — since the apostle himself and Titus and the rest were formerly just such persons, and should not glory over them or treat them contemptuously. Add the theological ground, that the same grace which made a difference in us could make one in these also, and may be made in God's own time. And on the following verse, mark that the kindness appeared when these persons were in the full career of sin, so that they had done no preparatory works and had no previous qualifications or dispositions for the grace of God.

Include the apostle without hesitation, and show how a man might belong in such a list while walking blameless as to the letter of the law: the manner in which he persecuted the Christians, to whose charge he could not lay one moral evil, is sufficient proof that his heart was in a state of great estrangement from God, from justice, holiness, mercy and compassion. Gloss the words in turn — foolish, that is without understanding, ignorant of God and his providence and his grace; disobedient, that is unpersuaded, unbelieving and obstinate; deceived, that is erring and wandering from the right way in consequence of our ignorance, and, in consequence of our unbelief and obstinacy, not choosing to know it. There are none so blind as those who will not see, and such persons are proof against conviction, being convinced neither by God nor man. Then make the strongest complaint of the chapter, that an attribute of the divine nature has been entirely lost by a paraphrastical translation: the word is philanthropy, a character which God here gives himself, and while human nature exists this must remain a character of the divine nature. God loved man when the idea was formed in his own infinite mind, formed him according to it and rejoiced in the work of his hands; and when man fell the same love devised his redemption, so that God the Saviour flows from God the Philanthropist.

debates.question: Does Paul include himself among the foolish and disobedient?

sides.position: No, not particularly: some things named here were probably not true of him, and the connexion does not require it
Yes, beyond doubt: his persecution of the Christians proves his heart estranged from God, though he walked blameless as to the letter of the law
He is classing himself for the moment with the people he describes — a rhetorical act, whose force would tell on Titus, himself of a Gentile family

debates.question: Does 'deceived' mean led astray by another, or going astray oneself?

sides.position: Led astray: by the great enemy, by false teachers, by our own hearts, by the flattery of others
Going astray, wandering from the road that leads to life — and, through unbelief, not choosing to know it
The participle is passive, though the middle is possible

outliers.note: Alone protests that a paraphrastical translation has lost an attribute of the divine nature, insisting the word is philanthropy, a character God gives himself, and that God the Saviour flows from God the Philanthropist.

Alone turns the verse into a discipline for the preacher, that he who remembers his own former life will exhort the wicked most effectually, and that a Christian tempted to unkind thoughts should reflect on his own past.

Alone considers the effect the argument would have on the man who had to deliver it, Titus being of a Gentile family and probably nurtured in idolatry, and alone describes the pleasures in view as those of a partly Greek, partly Asiatic people whose revellings wore a thin veil of false refinement.

themes: For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
But after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared,

5.pericope_label: Not by works of righteousness, but by the washing of regeneration

schools.summary: State the exclusion of works as a fundamental principle: they come in for no share in the justification of the soul and are in no sense a consideration on account of which God pardons, so that after all our tears and prayers and good deeds salvation remains a mere favour which God might justly withhold with no blame attaching to him. Then be exact about what the denial does not say: it does not assert that such works were ever done and found insufficient, only that to win salvation such must be done, and sad experience has shown the impossibility of any of us, even the holiest, doing the works of a purely righteous man for a single day. On the washing, two courses are open and both must be argued. Either take the noun to mean a bath rather than a laver, allow that it would naturally be understood of baptism, and then draw the line hard — baptism is the emblem, not the means, of purifying the soul; it is nowhere taught in the New Testament that baptism is regeneration; the word occurs only here and in one place where it indubitably does not refer to baptism; its correlatives are applied only to the moral change produced by the Spirit; and the usage leaves the impression that the only change needful is that which accompanies a regular baptism, on which point so much injury has been done in the church. Or hold that the laver can only signify the baptismal font, that by means of it God has put us into a state of salvation, and that baptism is the means through which we receive the saving grace of Christ — taking baptism always in its completion, the outward sign accompanied by inward grace, with repentance and faith required of one come to years of understanding and, in infants, the same profession made by sureties. On the outpouring, either refer it to the great Pentecost as foretold by the prophet, or deny any particular allusion to that day, the sense being that the Spirit has been imparted richly to all converted at any time or place. And divide the following verse among the three Persons: the Father pours out the Spirit, the Son's atonement makes it possible, the Spirit builds up the new life — noting that Saviour, applied to the Father a verse earlier, is here given to the Son, the Father being architect of our salvation and the Son its builder.

Take the justification as the second way by which God saves his people, since he saves no unjustified ones and none who are without the robe of Christ's righteousness. Distinguish carefully what kind of justification is meant: it is an act of God's gracious will conceived in his mind from eternity, by which he wills not to impute sin to his people but to Christ their surety; it was pronounced on Christ as their head and representative at his resurrection, when he was justified and discharged and they in him; and what takes place in regeneration is declarative only, since regeneration justifies no one but makes the justified appear to be such. On the sixth verse, take what was shed abundantly to be the Spirit himself with his gifts and graces — faith, hope and love and every other — poured forth in great abundance where sin had abounded.

Argue the exclusion from the catalogue just given: those who were foolish and deceived and serving divers lusts could have no works of righteousness to plead, so if saved at all it must be by mercy. On the washing, say undoubtedly the apostle here means baptism, the rite by which persons were admitted into the Church and the visible sign of the cleansing influences of the Holy Spirit; and then hold both ends at once, which is the whole difficulty. Baptism is only a sign, and therefore should never be separated from the thing signified; but it is a rite commanded by God himself, and therefore the thing signified should never be expected without it. By the renewing of the Holy Ghost understand not merely the profession of being bound to live a new life but the grace that renews the heart and enables us so to live. Baptism changes nothing; the grace signified by it cleanses and purifies; and they who think baptism to be regeneration neither know the Scriptures nor the power of God, but do greatly err. On the outpouring, hear baptism still in the verb and make the manner do the work: since the water was sometimes only sprinkled on the person, the heavenly gift was poured out not in drops but richly. And add that baptism is nothing in itself, since there had been no outpouring of the Spirit had there been no saving and atoning Christ.

Read the verse as promise rather than as argument, and let the prophets carry it: may these words be spoken now over you also, Sing, O heavens, and be joyful, O earth, for the Lord hath had mercy on his people and comforted the lowly of his people. This shall come to pass through the loving-kindness of God, who says, Behold, I will blot out as a cloud thy transgressions and as a thick cloud thy sins. Then take up the apostle's own words — that being justified by his grace we might be made heirs according to hope of eternal life — and turn them into prayer: may God himself, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give unto you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of himself, the eyes of your understanding being enlightened, and may he ever keep you in good works and words.

debates.question: What is the washing of regeneration?

sides.position: The emblem of regeneration, not its means; it is nowhere taught that baptism is regeneration, and the usage has done great injury in the church
Undoubtedly baptism, but only a sign: it should never be separated from the thing signified, nor the thing signified expected without it — baptism changes nothing
The baptismal font: baptism is the means through which we receive the saving grace of Christ, taken always in its completion, outward sign with inward grace

debates.question: Does the outpouring of the Spirit refer to Pentecost?

sides.position: Yes: the reference is to the great Pentecost, as foretold by the prophet
No particular allusion here to that day; the Spirit has been imparted richly to all converted at any time or place

outliers.note: Alone assembles a five-fold case against applying the word regeneration to baptism — from the word's proper meaning, from the absence of Scripture usage, from the context, from its correlatives, and from the danger — and reads the following clause as Paul's own guard against the error.

Alone takes the laver as the means rather than the emblem, while defining baptism throughout as the outward sign accompanied by inward grace, and alone provides for the case of infants, whose profession is made by sureties and publicly assented to at years of discretion.
Alone makes the manner of the outpouring do exegetical work, observing that since the baptismal water was sometimes only sprinkled, the heavenly gift is said to be poured out not in drops but richly.

themes: Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Which he shed on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour;
That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

8.pericope_label: A faithful saying: that they be careful to maintain good works

schools.summary: Refer the faithful saying to what has just been said, that the doctrine stated about the method of salvation is in the highest degree important and entirely worthy of belief. Then widen the good works rather than narrowing them: they refer not merely to acts of benevolence and charity but to all that is upright and good, to an honest and holy life. And say why the doctrines are to be constantly taught — they were no matters of speculation but were fitted to promote human happiness, and the doctrines of the gospel are suited to lead men to holy living.

Take the phrase to mean this is the true doctrine, the doctrine that cannot fail, and render the next clause as a desire that Titus maintain earnestly what concerns these points. Then enumerate what those points are, since the reference is to all that has just been written: the ruined state of man in soul and body; the infinite goodness of God which devised his salvation; the manifestation of that goodness in the incarnation of Jesus Christ; the justification which believers receive through his blood; the mission of the Holy Spirit and the purification of the heart by his influence; the hope of the resurrection of the body and the final glorification of both body and soul; and the necessity of obedience to the will of God. All these Titus is to press continually on the attention of believers, keeping constantly in view that all good comes from God's infinite kindness by and through Christ Jesus. Add who is meant by those that have believed: all Christians, for who can maintain good works but those who have the principle from which good works flow?

Set the foolish questions against the state of things in Crete and the many judaizers there, distinguishing needful questions, which make for improvement in useful knowledge, from idle enquiries tending neither to God's glory nor the edification of men, which may have a show of wisdom but are vain. On the genealogies, canvass both the genealogies of the gods that the heathen poets made such noise about and those the Jews were curious in; allow that some enquiry into the latter is lawful, to see the fulfilling of the scriptures in the descent of the Messiah; but condemn what serves pomp only and feeds vanity in a long pedigree, the more so since the distinction of families and tribes had been taken away, so that to pursue them is to build again a policy now abolished. On the heretic, give the image that carries the weight: he is subverted, a metaphor from a building so ruined as to make it difficult if not impossible to repair and raise it up again, and real heretics have seldom been recovered to the true faith — not so much from defect of judgment as from perverseness of the will, through pride or ambition or self-willedness. Then be careful on both sides: real heresy is not lightly to be charged upon any, though greatly to be taken heed of by all; pains and patience must be used, and such are not easily to be given up; the church's means even with heretics are persuasive and rational, for they must be admonished and instructed and warned. And explain the self-condemnation as an act, since those who will not be reclaimed inflict upon themselves the punishment the governors of the church should inflict, throwing themselves out of her communion.

Read the charge as an exhortation to almsgiving in particular. Having considered the care and exceeding love of God for man, the apostle thence exhorts to it, and not in a common or slight manner but that they may be careful to maintain it — succouring the injured not only by money but by patronage and protection, defending the widows and the orphans, affording a refuge to all that are afflicted; for this is to maintain good works. On the genealogies, glance at the Jews, who, priding themselves on having Abraham for their forefather, neglected their own part; and call such things foolish because it is the part of folly to confide in things unprofitable. Then face the difficulty the next verse raises, since the same apostle elsewhere says that God may peradventure give them repentance. In the former passage he speaks of the correction of those of whom he had hope, who had simply made opposition; but when a man is perverted and predetermined not to change his mind whatever may happen, and is known and manifest to all, why labour in vain, sowing upon a rock, why beat the air, when that honourable toil might be spent upon thy own people? And explain the last phrase by evidence: he cannot say that no one told him or admonished him, and since after admonition he continues the same, he is self-condemned.

debates.question: What are the good works Titus is to affirm constantly?

sides.position: Almsgiving in particular: succouring the injured by money, patronage and protection, defending widows and orphans, affording refuge to the afflicted
Not merely acts of benevolence and charity, but all that is upright and good — an honest and holy life

debates.question: In what sense is the heretic self-condemned?

sides.position: By evidence: he cannot plead that no one told or admonished him, and since after admonition he continues the same, he condemns himself
By act: such men inflict on themselves the punishment the church's governors should inflict, throwing themselves out of her communion

outliers.note: Alone states and answers the tension between this command and the apostle's counsel elsewhere that God may peradventure grant repentance, distinguishing those of whom there is still hope from the man known and manifest to all — with whom to contend is sowing upon a rock and beating the air.

Alone enumerates what 'these things' comprehends, running from the ruined state of man through the incarnation, justification, the mission of the Spirit and the hope of the resurrection to the necessity of obedience, as the sum of what Titus is to press continually.

Alone supplies the metaphor behind 'subverted', a building so ruined that it is difficult if not impossible to raise up again, and alone locates the cause of heresy in perverseness of will rather than defect of judgment, while insisting the charge is not lightly to be made.

themes: This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.

10.pericope_label: A man that is an heretick, after the first and second admonition, reject

schools.summary: Rest the definition on the word itself, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and on the related noun, which elsewhere is rendered sect. The true notion is one who is a promoter of a sect or party: the man who makes divisions in a church instead of aiming to promote unity, who may form parties on some point of doctrine, or on a custom or religious rite, making some unimportant matter a ground of distinction and endeavouring to get up a new organization. Such a man is a heretic by scriptural usage, and not merely one who holds a doctrine different from what is regarded as orthodoxy. The other Pauline uses of the cognate noun confirm it, for in neither does the word signify a fundamental or doctrinal error, that sense belonging to a usage of later times. Reconstruct the man accordingly: dissatisfied with the organisation and discipline Titus had introduced, not improbably considering himself in some way slighted, he withdrew from the common body and gathered other discontented spirits into what might be termed a rival Church — and note that even where no marked erroneous teaching is present at first, such small rival communities tend ever more to distinguish their teaching from the larger body they left. Then set out what rejection permits, and set out its limits in order. The utmost allowed is mere exclusion; we may not follow the offender with injury; we are not authorized to oppose a man for his mere private opinions; it does not make it right to deliver him over to the secular arm, or to harm him in body, soul, property or reputation, and it gives no power to torture him on the rack or to bind him to the stake. We may decline to recognise him as a Christian brother or to admit him to office, and beyond this there is no right to go, since he has a right to his own opinion still so far as we are concerned. Render the verb shun or avoid, and let the contumacious man be left simply to his own devices; and take the strong word in the last verse literally, that he has been turned inside out, finding the self-condemnation in this, that after warning he is without the excuse of ignorance and his stirring up of party-feeling convicts him of the very wrong he professes to condemn.

Give both senses of the word and decline to choose between them. A heretic is either one who makes choice of an opinion upon his own judgment, contrary to the generally received sense of the churches of Christ, prefers it to theirs and obstinately persists in it, separating from them and forming a party at whose head he sets himself; or he is one who removes and takes away a fundamental doctrine of Christianity, which affects particularly the doctrine of the Trinity and the deity and personality of Father, Son and Spirit, and especially the doctrines relating to the person, office and grace of Christ. Then distinguish the two terms carefully, for though schism and heresy differ, and every schismatic may not be a heretic, yet every heretic is a schismatic: he makes a rent in the doctrine of Christ and makes parties and divisions in his church. And say what follows practically — such are not always to be contended and disputed with, but to be avoided and rejected.

Define the man generally as one obstinately attached to an opinion contrary to the peace and comfort of society, who will submit neither to Scripture nor to reason; then identify him here as a person who maintains Judaism in opposition to Christianity, or who insists on the necessity of circumcision in order to be saved. Then put the question that the history of the church makes unavoidable. Labour to convince him of his error; but if he will not receive instruction, if he have shut his heart against conviction, then — burn him alive? No: even if demonstrably a heretic in any sense of that word, and a disturber of the peace of the Church, God gives no man any other authority over him but to shun him. Do him no harm in body, soul, character or substance; hold no communion with him; but leave him to God. On the last verse, read the self-condemnation as a matter of motive rather than of evidence: it refers to the Judaizing teacher who maintained his party and opinions for filthy lucre's sake, and who was conscious of his own insincerity, proclaiming his system not from a conscientious love of truth but from a desire to get his livelihood. And add the application, that were the Church in all countries, whether established by law or unestablished, strictly scrutinized, multitudes of heretics of this kind would be found.

debates.question: What makes a man a heretic?

sides.position: Factiousness, not doctrine: he is a promoter of a sect or party, one who makes divisions instead of promoting unity
A withdrawal from the body over discipline, by one who thought himself slighted and gathered discontented spirits into a rival Church
Either an opinion obstinately preferred to the churches', or the removal of a fundamental doctrine touching the Trinity or the person of Christ
Here, one who maintains Judaism in opposition to Christianity, or insists on the necessity of circumcision in order to be saved

debates.question: In what sense is such a man 'condemned of himself'?

sides.position: He is without the excuse of ignorance after warning, and his stirring up of party-feeling convicts him of the very wrong he professes to condemn
He is conscious of his own insincerity, maintaining his party for filthy lucre's sake rather than from a love of truth

outliers.note: Alone enumerates the limits of what rejection permits — no injury, no opposition for private opinion, no delivery to the secular arm, no rack and no stake — concluding that the utmost allowed is mere exclusion and that the man has a right to his own opinion still.

Alone puts the question bluntly as history had answered it, asking whether the obstinate man is to be burnt alive and replying that God gives no authority over him but to shun him; and alone reads the self-condemnation as a matter of motive, the Judaizing teacher conscious of maintaining his party for his livelihood.

Alone explains why the disturber is left nameless, partly from a loving hope that Titus would win him and partly because the letter was public instruction to many a church besides Crete's; and alone observes that rival communities drift into distinctive teaching even where none was present at first.

themes: A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself.

12.pericope_label: Bring Zenas and Apollos on their journey: let ours also learn to maintain good works

schools.summary: Say what is known of the three names and, more importantly, what is not. Of Artemas nothing certainly is known, though tradition makes him afterwards a bishop; Tychicus appears in several New Testament writings and seems to have been among the most esteemed of Paul's friends, spoken of as a beloved brother and faithful minister, the importance of his missions showing how high he stood. Of Zenas nothing is known beyond this place; the term lawyer might indicate a Roman jurist, but the law in which he was expert was more likely that of Moses, and it does not mean he practised law in the modern sense. On Apollos be full: a distinguished Alexandrian scholar converted by Priscilla and Aquila, who might have rivalled or even superseded Paul in authority over the churches of the Mediterranean seaboard, but resolutely declined any such rivalry and lived as his loyal friend, Paul always treating him as an equal power and classing him with Peter and himself. Report Luther's suggestion that Apollos wrote the epistle to the Hebrews, whose authorship has been disputed as far back as Origen; and note the remarkable fact that these three friends, named in almost the last epistle Paul wrote, all bear names derived from famous heathen deities. On Nicopolis, list the cities of that name and judge the one in Epirus most likely, built after the battle from which it took its name. Read the recall as a reminder that Titus is only the temporary ruler of the Cretan Church on a special commission. And on the last charge, allow that the Greek will admit or include the marginal rendering about honest trades, but see no reason why the direction should have any peculiar reference to them, wishing rather that Christians generally be characterized by good works of all kinds.

Weigh what kind of lawyer Zenas was, since the versions differ. Whether he was brought up to the civil law among the Greeks or Romans is not certain; it may be he was a Jewish lawyer or scribe, an interpreter of the law of Moses, for with the Jews a lawyer and a scribe were one and the same, and one version here calls him a scribe while another calls him a scribe of the city, which looks as if it were a civil office. Be that as it may, he seems to have been by now a preacher of the Gospel, being joined with Apollos, who certainly was one. On the last charge, deny that honest trades alone are meant, while granting that a trade is a work and an honest lawful employment a good work, which ought to be learnt in order to be followed — the Jews saying that he who does not teach his son a trade is as if he taught him to rob, so that their doctors were brought up to trades, as the Apostle Paul was though he had an education under Gamaliel. Then list the uses such an employment serves: the good of a man's self, the supply of his family, the assistance of others in need, the support of the Gospel, and the relief of poor saints, that such may not be unfruitful and useless in commonwealths, neighbourhoods, churches and families.

Fix the geography, and then use one word to fix the chronology. Nicopolis was a city of Epirus on the gulf of Ambracia near Actium, which Augustus built in commemoration of his victory over Mark Antony; there was another of the same name in Thrace, but the former is the place intended, and the subscription at the end of the epistle should not be trusted, none of those subscriptions being of any authority. Now observe that the apostle says he has determined THERE to winter, not here: hence he was certainly not yet arrived, it was probably now pretty late in the autumn, and he was drawing near — so that this letter was not written from Nicopolis at all. Note also that his spending the winter at this or any other practicable place depended on his own determination, so that he was at liberty. On Titus himself, say that he was properly an evangelist, who by the nature of that office had no fixed residence but presided over other elders wherever he travelled, assisting each of the apostles according to the measure of his abilities; and that Artemas or Tychicus was to succeed him in his office. On the journey, explain the practice: the churches through which these evangelists passed bore their expenses from one to the next, so Titus is to afford them the means of defraying theirs.

Keep the practical charge in view at the close: Christianity is not a fruitless profession, and its professors must be filled with the fruits of righteousness which are by Jesus Christ, doing good as well as keeping away from evil. Let ours follow some honest labour and employment, to provide for themselves and their families, since Christianity obliges all to it. And on the arrangements, note why the apostle would not have the Cretan churches left without oversight: they were young and weak, and should not be without one or other of chief sufficiency to guide and help them, which is why Titus was not to leave until Artemas or Tychicus had come to supply his place.

debates.question: Was the epistle written from Nicopolis?

sides.position: Probably it was written there
No: he says he has determined THERE to winter, not here, so he had not yet arrived and the letter was not written from thence

debates.question: Does 'let ours learn to maintain good works' mean to profess honest trades?

sides.position: The Greek will admit or include it, but the direction has no peculiar reference to trades; Christians generally should be marked by good works of all kinds
Not trades only, though a trade is a good work and ought to be learnt in order to be followed
Let ours follow some honest labour and employment, to provide for themselves and their families

outliers.note: Alone notices that the three friends named in almost the last epistle Paul wrote all bear names derived from famous heathen deities, and alone reports Luther's suggestion that Apollos was the unknown writer of the epistle to the Hebrews, whose authorship had been disputed as far back as Origen.

Alone dismisses the subscriptions appended to Paul's epistles as of no authority, and so sets aside the traditional identification of Nicopolis; and alone defines the office Titus held, an evangelist with no fixed residence who presided over elders wherever he travelled.

Alone explains the arrangement behind the request, that the churches through which evangelists passed bore their travelling expenses from one to the next; and alone dates the letter from the word 'there', inferring that it was late in the autumn and the apostle still on his way.

themes: When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus, be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis: for I have determined there to winter.
Bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them.
And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.

All that are with me salute thee. Greet them that love us in the faith. Grace be with you all. Amen.  It was written to Titus, ordained the first bishop of the church of the Cretians, from Nicopolis of Macedonia.
